title: What is String interning, and how does it affect == comparisons (literals vs new String(...) vs .intern())?
shortTitle: What is String interning and how it affects == comparisons

s1_definition.profdef: String interning is the process of storing exactly one canonical copy of each distinct string value in the String Pool and returning that shared reference for equal values. Literals are interned automatically, so identical literals share one object and compare equal with `==`. A string created with `new String(...)` is a distinct heap object that is not interned, so it does not share identity with the literal and `==` returns false. Calling `.intern()` returns the canonical pooled reference for the value, so after interning, `==` against a literal of the same value returns true. Interning therefore controls object identity, which is exactly what `==` compares, while value equality via `.equals()` is unaffected.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, interning is like head office keeping one official master card per account label and insisting everyone use that single card. When a clerk writes a brand-new card by hand with new String, it is a separate card, so comparing it by "is this the very same card" says no, even though the writing matches. If the clerk submits the card to head office with intern, head office hands back the one official master card, and now the identity check says yes. The words on the card, the value, were always equal; interning only changes whether everyone is holding the exact same physical card.
s1_definition.oneliner: Interning stores one canonical object per value; literals are auto-interned so == is true, new String is distinct so == is false, and .intern() returns the shared reference so == becomes true.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** String interning is the process of storing exactly one canonical copy of each distinct string value in the String Pool and returning that shared reference for equal values. Literals are interned automatically, so identical literals share one object and compare equal with `==`. A string created with `new String(...)` is a distinct heap object that is not interned, so it does not share identity with the literal and `==` returns false. Calling `.intern()` returns the canonical pooled reference for the value, so after interning, `==` against a literal of the same value returns true. Interning therefore controls object identity, which is exactly what `==` compares, while value equality via `.equals()` is unaffected.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, interning is like head office keeping one official master card per account label and insisting everyone use that single card. When a clerk writes a brand-new card by hand with new String, it is a separate card, so comparing it by "is this the very same card" says no, even though the writing matches. If the clerk submits the card to head office with intern, head office hands back the one official master card, and now the identity check says yes. The words on the card, the value, were always equal; interning only changes whether everyone is holding the exact same physical card.

**One line to remember:** Interning stores one canonical object per value; literals are auto-interned so == is true, new String is distinct so == is false, and .intern() returns the shared reference so == becomes true.

sections.s2_technical:
Interning is about identity, not value. The String Pool holds one canonical String per distinct value. When a string is interned, future requests for the same value return that one shared object.

Literals are interned at class load. So if you write the literal SAV2001 twice, both references point to the same pooled object, and double-equals is true because they are literally the same object. This is a direct consequence of immutability plus pooling: it is safe to share because the string can never change.

A string built with new String is explicitly a new object. Even though its characters equal the literal, it is a separate instance on the heap, outside the pool. So double-equals between a new String and the literal is false, while equals is true because equals compares characters. This is the classic trap that causes bugs when developers use double-equals to compare strings that came from different sources.

The intern method bridges runtime strings to the pool. Calling intern on any string returns the canonical pooled reference for its value. If the pool already contains that value, you get the existing shared object; if not, the value is added and you get it back. So after calling intern on a new String of SAV2001, comparing the interned result with the literal by double-equals is true, because both now refer to the one pooled object.

A senior nuance is why this matters and when to use it. Interning is a memory and sometimes a speed optimization for many repeated equal strings, and it enables double-equals comparisons which are faster than equals, which some high-performance code exploits for a bounded set of known values like enums-as-strings. But over-interning dynamic strings wastes pool memory and can hurt performance. The disciplined rule is to compare string values with equals for correctness and to treat interning as a deliberate optimization, never as the basis of program logic. Another nuance is that interning identity is per JVM and per class loader context, so you should not rely on it across process boundaries or serialization.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A reconciliation bug at the National Bank rejected a valid match because it compared an account number from a database read, built with new String, against a literal using double-equals, which returned false. This is exactly the identity difference interning explains.

Problem 2 — The fix is to compare with equals for correctness, and optionally to intern a bounded set of status codes so that fast double-equals comparisons are valid. This is exactly the correct use of equals and deliberate interning.

Problem 3 — The team demonstrates all three cases, literal, new String, and intern, with double-equals and equals side by side. This is exactly the comparison the question asks for.

The code has a `StatusCodes` helper that interns a bounded set of codes, and a `StringInternDemo` main class contrasting the comparisons.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the literal SAV2001, a new String of SAV2001 simulating a database read, its interned form, and repeated COMPLETED status codes.

Step 1: The literal SAV2001 is interned automatically at class load and points to the one pooled object.

Step 2: The new String of SAV2001 is created as a distinct heap object, outside the pool, even though its characters match the literal.

Step 3: Comparing the literal and the new String with double-equals returns false, because they are different objects. This is the reconciliation bug in miniature.

Step 4: Comparing them with equals returns true, because equals compares characters, which are identical. This is the correct way to compare the values.

Step 5: Calling intern on the new String returns the pooled reference, so comparing the interned result with the literal by double-equals now returns true, because both refer to the single pooled object.

Step 6: Two separate COMPLETED strings are canonicalized through intern, both resolving to the one pooled COMPLETED, so double-equals between them, and against the literal COMPLETED, is true, which makes fast identity comparison valid for this bounded set of status codes.

```text
WARNING: literal == fromDb   : false
INFO: literal .equals fromDb : true
INFO: literal == interned    : true
INFO: canonical status == : true
INFO: is COMPLETED (fast==): true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  "SAV2001" literal ────────► Pool @P1  (auto-interned)
  new String("SAV2001") ────► Heap @H1  (NOT pooled)

  literal == fromDb  → @P1 vs @H1 → FALSE
  literal .equals fromDb → chars match → TRUE
  fromDb.intern() → returns @P1
  literal == interned → @P1 vs @P1 → TRUE

  intern("COMPLETED") (twice) → both → Pool @P2
     s1 == s2 → TRUE ;  s1 == "COMPLETED" → TRUE (fast identity)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Reconciliation with Correct String Comparison ═══

  ┌────────────┐  DB reads ┌──────────────────┐  compare ┌──────────────┐
  │ Bank feed  │─────────→ │ Reconciliation    │────────→ │ Match report │
  │ (new Strs) │           │ uses .equals()    │          └──────────────┘
  └────────────┘           │ interns status codes│
                           └──────────────────┘
  Correctness: .equals() for values; intern only bounded status codes

```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Interning and == ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Source of string        in pool?   == literal? │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ literal "X"               YES         TRUE      │
  │ "A"+"B" const fold        YES         TRUE      │
  │ new String("X")           NO          FALSE     │
  │ runtime var concat        NO          FALSE     │
  │ anyString.intern()        YES         TRUE      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Rules:
   == tests IDENTITY (same object) — changed by interning
   .equals tests VALUE — NEVER changed by interning
   correctness → use .equals()
   optimization → intern a BOUNDED known set, then == is valid & fast
   caution → do not intern unbounded dynamic strings (pool bloat)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
String interning is the process of keeping exactly one canonical copy of each distinct string value in the String Pool and returning that shared reference whenever an equal value is requested. The crucial thing to understand is that interning is about object identity, and double-equals compares identity, so interning directly changes what double-equals reports, while the equals method, which compares characters, is completely unaffected.

Literals are interned automatically at class load, so two identical literals point to the same pooled object and double-equals between them is true. A string built with new String is deliberately a distinct object on the heap, outside the pool, so even though its characters equal the literal, double-equals with the literal is false, while equals is true. That mismatch is the classic bug: comparing strings from different sources with double-equals and getting the wrong answer. The intern method bridges a runtime string to the pool, returning the canonical pooled reference for its value, so after interning a new String of a value, double-equals against a literal of the same value becomes true.

I ran into exactly this in a reconciliation job. An account number read from the database was a new String, and comparing it to a literal with double-equals returned false, which rejected a valid match. The fix had two parts. For correctness, I always compare string values with equals, never double-equals. As an optional optimization, for a bounded, known set of values like status codes, I deliberately intern them so that fast double-equals identity comparisons become valid, which is the same idea behind treating a small fixed set of strings almost like enum constants.

The senior points I always add are that interning is a deliberate memory and sometimes speed optimization, that over-interning unbounded dynamic strings bloats the pool and can hurt performance, and that interning identity is per JVM, so I never rely on it across process boundaries or serialization. In short, I use equals for logic and treat interning purely as a controlled optimization for repeated or bounded values.
